client: I’ve been really anxious about this networking event coming up next week. Every time I think about introducing myself to strangers in my field, my heart starts racing, and I feel like I’m going to freeze up or say something stupid. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like it’s just who I am, and I don’t know if I can change that.
therapist: It sounds like this upcoming event is really stirring up some intense worry for you, especially around how others might perceive you. The way your voice tightens when you talk about it makes me think this fear feels very real and overwhelming right now. Let’s explore together whether these thoughts about "being this way forever" are facts or just very convincing feelings.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I know logically that I won't feel this anxious forever, but in the moment it really does feel permanent. The worst part is that even if I get through this event okay, I keep imagining all the future events where I'll feel just as panicked. It's like my brain won't let me believe things could ever be different.
therapist: I hear how trapped you feel between your logical understanding and these intense, future-focused worries—your voice sounds both rushed and deflated, like this cycle is exhausting you. That sense of permanence you're describing is actually a very common trick anxiety plays on us, making temporary feelings seem like unchangeable truths. Would it help to look at how your past experiences with anxiety might show a different pattern than what your worries are predicting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about anxiety making things feel permanent, but when I'm in that panicked state, it really does feel like this is just how life will always be. I can think of times when my worries didn't come true, but in the moment that doesn't seem to help - it's like my brain just finds new things to panic about.
therapist: Your voice has that strained quality as you describe this, like you're holding both frustration and exhaustion about this cycle—it makes complete sense that past successes feel irrelevant when anxiety takes over. That feeling of your brain constantly finding new worries is actually anxiety's way of trying to protect you, even though it ends up trapping you instead. What if we looked at these panicked moments not as failures, but as opportunities to practice responding differently to those alarm bells?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I guess I do feel exhausted by it. It’s like no matter how many times I handle something okay, the next worry pops up and I’m back to square one. I hear what you’re saying about seeing it as an opportunity, but it’s hard to think that way in the moment. When I’m panicking, it feels like everything is falling apart, and I can’t just flip a switch to see it differently.
therapist: I hear that weariness in your voice—it's softer and faster now, like you're carrying the weight of all these repeated cycles. That sense of "back to square one" must feel so discouraging when you've put in so much effort already. Let's honor how real that struggle is while also gently challenging whether "falling apart" is the only possible story your panic gets to tell.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I do feel stuck in this cycle, like no matter how many breathing exercises I try or positive thoughts I force, the panic always comes back. Part of me wants to believe there's another way to see this, but another part is just so tired of trying things that don't seem to stick. 

When you say "falling apart isn't the only story," it makes me defensive—because in the moment, it really does feel like the only possible outcome. How do I even begin to imagine another version when my body's screaming that disaster is coming?
therapist: Your voice speeds up and pitches higher as you describe this struggle—it’s clear how deeply frustrating and exhausting this cycle feels for you, especially when the tools you’ve tried haven’t brought the relief you hoped for. That defensiveness you mention makes complete sense—it’s hard to trust in another possibility when your body feels flooded with panic. What if we shifted focus from trying to "fix" the panic in the moment to simply noticing it with curiosity, as uncomfortable as it is, to see if that changes how you relate to it over time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about noticing the panic instead of trying to fix it, but it feels almost impossible in the moment. When I’m in that state, all I want is for it to stop—it’s so overwhelming that the idea of just sitting with it seems counterintuitive, like I’m giving in to it. Plus, I’ve tried mindfulness before, and it always feels like I’m doing it wrong or it’s not helping. What if it just makes things worse?
therapist:
Your voice sounds both weary and hesitant—almost deflated—as you talk about these attempts, like you’ve been let down by so many approaches that even the suggestion of mindfulness brings up frustration and doubt. That fear of making things worse by "sitting with it" is completely understandable when panic feels so urgent and overwhelming in the moment. 

Instead of framing it as something you have to "do right," what if we thought of it more like turning down the volume on a radio—not trying to shut it off completely, but just noticing when the panic station gets louder and softer without fighting it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about turning down the volume, but it still feels like panic is this huge, uncontrollable force. When it hits, it’s like everything else disappears, and it’s hard to even remember to "notice" anything. I’ve tried mindfulness apps and breathing exercises before, but they just made me more frustrated because I couldn’t calm down fast enough. It feels like I’m failing at it every time.
therapist: Your voice sounds quieter and higher-pitched, like you’re carrying both frustration and a sense of defeat about these attempts—it’s clear how much effort you’ve put into trying to manage this, only to feel like it’s not working. That feeling of panic being an "uncontrollable force" must make it so hard to trust in any approach right now. What if we shifted the goal from "calming down fast enough" to simply noticing whether the panic feels any different when you’re not fighting it so hard?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about not fighting the panic, but that's easier said than done. When it hits, it feels like my whole body is screaming at me to DO something, not just sit there noticing it. And honestly, the idea of not trying to calm down kind of scares me - what if it just keeps getting worse?
therapist: Your voice sounds both tense and a little shaky as you describe this—like you’re holding onto a real fear that stepping back from the fight might let the panic swallow you whole. That instinct to *do something* makes complete sense when your body’s screaming danger, even if the fighting itself is exhausting. What if we thought of this less as passive surrender and more like learning to float in rough water—not trying to calm the waves, but discovering you can stay afloat even when they’re crashing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about floating instead of fighting, but the waves feel so overwhelming right now. When I try to just let the anxiety be there, it feels like I'm drowning - like if I stop struggling, I'll just sink. I don't know if I can trust that I'll naturally float like you're suggesting.
therapist: Your voice rises sharply when you talk about drowning—I can hear how viscerally terrifying that surrender feels, like letting go for even a moment might mean being swallowed up completely. That lack of trust in your ability to float makes so much sense when every survival instinct is screaming to thrash against the waves. Would it help to start smaller—not expecting to float through the whole storm, but just noticing if there are moments when the water feels slightly easier to bear when you’re not fighting so hard?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know about "smaller moments"... when I'm in that panicked state, it feels like it's all or nothing. Either I'm completely drowning or I'm not. The idea of trying to notice little respites sounds nice in theory, but in the moment it's like my brain just can't access that kind of subtle awareness. Everything feels urgent and life-or-death.
therapist: Your voice sounds both rushed and quieter now, like you're describing something that feels impossibly big and overwhelming in the moment—it’s clear how all-consuming that "all or nothing" panic feels for you. That sense of urgency and life-or-death intensity makes it so hard to slow down and notice anything subtle. What if we thought of this less as trying to find respites in the moment and more like practicing noticing small shifts *after* the wave has passed—like looking back at a storm and seeing where it might have eased, even briefly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
